summary:
Simon Willison's talk covers several open challenges in AI engineering. He begins by describing the 'GPT-4 barrier' — the roughly 12-month period when GPT-4 was uncontested, which has now ended with models from Anthropic, Google, Meta, and others competing at the top tier. He presents rebuilt versions of benchmark-vs-cost charts and animated LMSYS Chatbot Arena rankings, criticizing MMLU as 'bar trivia' and favoring ELO-based 'vibes' rankings. Open-source models like Llama 3 70B and Chinese models from Alibaba and DeepSeek AI now reach GPT-4 class. He notes GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet are effectively free to consumers, citing Ethan Mollick's observation that free 'bad AI' caused people to miss the technology's potential. He argues ChatGPT is deceptively hard to use, illustrating with opaque PDF handling behavior that depends on searchability, length, tables, and code interpreter packages — making these power-user tools requiring significant experience.

He then addresses the AI trust crisis, citing Dropbox and Slack user panics over data training that wasn't happening. Anthropic proves great models don't need customer data, but committed the 'original sin' of training on unlicensed web scrapes, complicating trust. He covers prompt injection extensively, highlighting the markdown image exfiltration bug found in six products (ChatGPT, Google Bard, writer.com, Amazon Q, Google Notebook LM, GitHub Co-pilot chat) where invisible markdown images can exfiltrate private data. He shares a humorous example where a RAG application ingested his release notes and adopted a 'witty Geral' persona, illustrating that LLMs are gullible. He defines 'slop' as AI-generated content that is both unrequested and unreviewed, comparing it to spam — before 'spam' entered common use, people didn't know unwanted marketing messages were bad. He argues humans must take accountability for published content, something LLMs can never do. He concludes with a call to action: establish responsible usage patterns and help everyone else adopt these tools.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: The GPT-4 Barrier
sections.summary: Willison explains he replaced OpenAI as speaker at the last minute. He introduces the GPT-4 barrier: GPT-4 was released in March last year and remained uncontested as the best model for 12 months, which he found disheartening for lack of competition.

sections.title: Model Landscape: Benchmarks and Cost
sections.summary: He presents a rebuilt version of Karina Wynn's MMLU vs cost chart, created with GPT-4 code interpreter. Three clusters emerge: top-tier GPT-4 class models, cheap models, and outdated GPT 3.5 Turbo which users should abandon.

sections.title: Vibes and the Chatbot Arena
sections.summary: He criticizes MMLU as 'bar trivia' and argues the LMSYS Chatbot Arena ELO rankings better capture real model quality ('vibes'). Open-source models like Llama 3 70B plus models from Nvidia, Cohere, Alibaba, and DeepSeek AI now compete in GPT-4 class.

sections.title: GPT-4 Class Models as Commodity
sections.summary: The GPT-4 barrier is decimated; four organizations now compete. GPT-4 class models are becoming a commodity. He cites Ethan Mollick on how free 'bad AI' caused people to miss the technology's potential, but now GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet are effectively free to consumers.

sections.title: ChatGPT Is Hard to Use
sections.summary: Despite seeming simple, ChatGPT is a power-user tool. The PDF upload example illustrates this: behavior varies by searchability, length, tables/diagrams, and which code interpreter packages are used. Like Excel, mastery takes years of experience.

sections.title: The AI Trust Crisis
sections.summary: Dropbox and Slack both faced user panics over AI features and data training concerns, but neither was actually training on customer data. Anthropic explicitly states they don't train on customer data, proving great models don't require it.

sections.title: Anthropic's Original Sin
sections.summary: Anthropic proved a great model can be trained without customer data, but they committed the 'original sin' of training on an unlicensed scrape of the entire web. This makes it difficult to convince users about data practices, since users can point out that AI companies already 'ripped off' their websites.

sections.title: Prompt Injection and Markdown Image Exfiltration
sections.summary: Willison insists everyone must understand prompt injection. He describes the markdown image exfiltration bug: a chatbot that renders markdown images can be tricked into exfiltrating private data via image links to attacker servers. Johan Raberger found this in GitHub Co-pilot chat. The same bug appeared in ChatGPT, Google Bard, writer.com, Amazon Q, Google Notebook LM, and GitHub Co-pilot chat — six talented teams making the identical mistake.

sections.title: Prompt Injection as a Bug: The Geral Example
sections.summary: Prompt injection isn't always a security hole — sometimes it's a funny bug. Someone built a RAG app tested against Willison's documentation; when asked 'what is the meaning of life,' it responded as a 'witty Geral' because Willison's release notes contained an example pretending to be one. This illustrates that LLMs are gullible — they believe anything from anyone, which is both a strength and a weakness.

sections.title: Slop and Accountability
sections.summary: Willison defines 'slop' as AI-generated content that is both unrequested and unreviewed. If you review AI-assisted content before publishing, that's not slop. He compares slop to spam — before 'spam' became common, people didn't know sending unwanted marketing messages was bad. He argues humans must take accountability for published content, something LLMs can never do since their output depends entirely on prompts.

sections.title: Call to Action: Responsible AI Use
sections.summary: GPT-4 class models are now free for everyone. Willison argues the audience — among the most qualified people to tackle these challenges — must do two things: establish patterns for responsible use (what's good, what's bad, what makes the world better), and help everyone else get on board. He closes by sharing his blog URLs.
